sheets.name: Read Me
rows: READ ME | Riverknoll feasibility model v19
Made Nov 25 2026 from v18 (v18 and earlier left unchanged). Blue cells are inputs, green cells link to another tab, black cells are formulas.
Long_Run: 60-year cash to RIT after debt and capital renewal (Gordian target), nominal and discounted payback, NPV and IRR for 513 and 444 beds.
Co_Benefits: retained tuition, lower housing cost for residents, trees, carbon, rain gardens and garden produce, priced from published sources; the rest listed as qualitative.
Total_Value: rent plus co-benefits over 60 years at 3%, 5.15% and 7%, and the co-benefits needed to break even.
Market_Impact: closure vs rebuild (513, 444, phased) effect on Henrietta rents, vacancies and non-student renters, with the evidence and its limits.
Sources: entries 31 onward added for v17.
Closure: RIT closes Riverknoll after spring 2027, so phases run continuously on the vacant site instead of 64–96 beds per summer (Assumptions row 24, Project_Timeline, Phased Rebuild).
Timeline: real dates from an authorization date (Assumptions!B38); phase count = new beds ÷ beds per phase, so 513 beds now fit the schedule (v15 fit only 384).
Costs: base building cost $300/GSF (was $425), contingency 15% (was 20%), tenting $0.5M (was $2M), checked against Lodge, Apex, SUNY and APX benchmarks (Benchmarks tab).
Escalation: now compounds from mid-2026 to each case's construction midpoint (Turner index), instead of a flat 6%.
Revenue: rent now counts new beds only (v15 counted all target beds) and is escalated to the year all phases open.
Debt: one basis for the whole model: A-rated 30-year muni rate 5.15% (FMS Bonds, Nov 24 2026), 1.20x coverage, $2,800/bed operating cost. Method selectable (Assumptions!B45).
Energy: all-electric heat pumps by default (NYS All-Electric Buildings Act; 2025 Energy Code). v15 assumed gas heat.
Accessibility: 5% single-level accessible homes and 2% communication units (ADA 233.3 via 28 CFR 36.406(e)); the drawn homes are all two-story walk-ups.
Area: compact 400 GSF/bed option added to test (Drawing Cost Basis rows 20–23); default stays the drawn 504.
New tabs: Market, Benchmarks, Capital Stack, Sources. 444-bed case added to Cost_Model (rows 14–16) and Summary row 19.
Bed target: v18 base 744 from demand (Demand tab); 444 floor and 871 high are modeled, with 513 kept for reference. Assumptions!B4.
Debt method: coverage test (recommended) or all NOI to debt service. Assumptions!B45.
Area per bed: drawn 504 GSF or a compact 400 GSF plan. Drawing Cost Basis!B18.
Retained 516–536: verified bed count needed (Assumptions!B5). Unknown whether RIT closes it too.
Funding: how much RIT capital, gifts or grants to target for the gap (Capital Stack rows 8–9).
Total project uses: $236,862,383 for 744 new beds ($318,363 per bed, nominal).
Break-even rent: $30,026 per bed-year vs $7,839 modeled in 2031.
First homes open Aug 2029; all open Aug 2031.
Demand: bed count derived from RIT Common Data Sets 2021-2025, housing capacity and occupancy, Riverknoll closure and five peer schools. Three methods give 444 / 748 / 871; base 744.

Layouts: all two-story homes vs a two-story + three-story mix vs all three-story at the base count, with cost, footprint, accessibility, zoning height and shadow. Assumptions!B58 picks the one Cost_Model uses (2 = mix).
Assumptions rows 56-68: three-story building inputs; B49 is now the blended GSF per bed and Cost_Model column F carries the blended $/GSF factor.
Bed rows in Cost_Model: 744 base, 871 high, 513 reference, 444 floor. Beds per phase 186 (four phases). Base-case labels on other tabs now follow Assumptions!B4.
Sources: entries 60 onward added for v18.

Townhome_Rows: the homes become 18 identical rows of 10 attached units (12 two-story with 4-bed townhomes, 6 three-story with 6-bed townhomes), each with two one-story accessible end units. Party walls and taller rows lower the $/GSF factor against v18’s detached homes. Assumptions!B58 = 4 uses it.
Building_Cost: one row, one townhome and a v18 detached home, cost layer by layer from the building itself to all-in.
Phasing: six phasing patterns at the same buildings; only inflation and financing change. Base is now 3 identical phases of 6 rows (Assumptions!C24 = 248).
Levers: walk from v18 to v19, then compact plan, off-site panels, overlapping phases, one drawing set and parking, alone and together.

Layouts column F adds the townhome rows beside the v18 layouts. System3E wall area now follows the rows (less exposed wall, so the wall-upgrade saving falls to about $7,400 a year). Sources: entries 81 onward added for v19.

RIT will close Riverknoll after spring 2027 (announced Nov 9 2026). Upperclass share housed rose 2.0 points in four years (CDS). Carry that rate to the planning year on flat enrollment.
C. Occupancy: house today's residents at normal occupancy
Capacity needed so 6,900 residents fill 94.5% of beds, less the capacity left after closure.
Recommended count (method B, rounded down to whole 12-bed buildings)
RIT share after the base case

1. RIT has housed about 6,500 undergraduates every fall since 2021 while its first-year class fell 8%. Upperclass students living on campus rose 7%, so demand for upperclass beds is growing on flat enrollment.
2. Housing is about full: 6,900 residents for 6,875 beds. Closing 444 Riverknoll beds without replacement cuts the share housed to 47.1%, the lowest in the series.
3. Method B gives 748 beds, so the base case is 744. That leaves RIT at 52.8% of undergrads housed, below the peer median of 60%, and housing about 96% full, near the national 94.5%.

4. Risks: enrollment is flat to slightly down and international students are falling (WXXI, Feb 2 2026); the trend is four data points. RIT's own waitlist and occupancy data would confirm or trim the count before Phase 4.
5. Site, cost and the courtyard design do not set this number. They are constraints, handled by the building mix (Layouts tab) and phasing.

Townhouse definition (IRC R202, 2015 wording): a single-family unit in a group of three or more attached units, each extending from foundation to roof, with a yard or public way on at least two sides. The residential code covers townhouses up to 3 stories with their own exit (IRC 101.2), so both row types qualify if each unit stays foundation-to-roof. Stephenville TX fire handout; NC OSFM interpretation Jan 30 2026.

Party walls (IRC R302.2): a common 1-hour wall when sprinklered, 2-hour when not, with no plumbing, ducts or vents inside it. NY 2025 code adds sprinklers to new townhouses on public water (NY DOS, Sept 2025), which points to the 1-hour wall. NY wording not yet read; architect to confirm.

Stacking units changes the code: stacked flats make the building multifamily (IBC R-2: NFPA 13R sprinklers, rated floors, fire alarm). v19 keeps every unit side by side so the rows stay townhouses; the one-story end units sit beside, not under, their neighbors.

Fair Housing Act: multistory townhouses in a building with no elevator are not covered; ground-floor units in a building of 4 or more units are. The one-story end units are single-level and accessible by design (HUD FAQ; 24 CFR 100 subpart D).
ADA at a school: 5% of beds in mobility-accessible units on an accessible route (2010 Standards 233.3). 36 end units give 72 accessible beds against 38 required, one pair in every row.

Height: two-story rows about 25 ft; three-story rows about 33 ft with a low-slope roof, under Henrietta’s 35 ft cap for schools but over the 2-story / 21 ft cap for plain residential buildings (§ 295-8). RIT’s zoning district still to confirm.
University use: if the code official treats RIT-leased townhomes as a dormitory (R-2), the rows are priced as commercial-code buildings and part of the saving is lost. Ask the Town and NY DOS early.

sheets.name: Phasing
rows: PHASING | does building in phases change the total? (v19)

Phasing splits the same buildings into smaller pieces; it does not make them cheaper. Each phase costs less, but the total stays the same in today’s dollars, and every extra year of building adds inflation (4.5% a year) on top. Since RIT closes Riverknoll after spring 2027, phasing no longer keeps students housed; it only spreads the spending. Restart costs per phase (mobilizing crews, cranes, site setup) are not priced here, so more phases are, if anything, understated.
v19 base: 3 phases, one at a time
v18 phasing: 4 phases, one at a time
6 smaller phases of 3 rows, one at a time
2 phases of 9 rows, one at a time
One phase: all 18 rows at once
Reading it: the cost before inflation is the same in every row. Only inflation and financing change, and they follow how long the money takes to go out.
More, smaller phases cost more (row 10): the work stretches out and inflation runs longer. Fewer or overlapping phases cost less but need more crews and more money at once.
Build months and gaps for rows 8-12 are assumptions for the construction manager to test; a 9-row or 18-row phase needs a larger contractor and supply chain.
Construction starts and design dates come from Project_Timeline (abatement month 12, first build month 14).

Tests the thesis that the closure pushes 400-500 students into the Henrietta rental market, raising rents and crowding out other renters, and that rebuilding relieves it. Evidence on student-housing changes specifically is weak; see the evidence table below.
